title: DHS Ends 'Duration of Status' for International Students, Imposing Four-Year Visa Caps
excerpt: The new rule replaces nearly 50 years of flexible student visa terms with fixed admission periods and USCIS-gated extensions, in a move economists warn could cost the U.S. up to $145 billion.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security published a rule on July 17 ending "duration of status" — the decades-old practice that let international students stay as long as their program lasted
  • F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors will now receive a maximum four-year admission, with costly USCIS applications required for extensions, school transfers, or program changes
  • A study commissioned by the National Academies estimates the rule could cost the U.S. economy $72–145 billion over ten years by deterring international talent
  • The change arrives as international student applications to U.S. universities have already dropped 20%, with India's share of STEM graduate students among the most affected populations

A Quiet Rule With Massive Reach

The Department of Homeland Security on July 17 finalized a regulation that eliminates "duration of status," a nearly 50-year-old policy that allowed international students, scholars, and medical trainees to remain in the United States for as long as they were enrolled in or completing their programs. The change replaces that flexibility with fixed admission periods of up to four years, after which students must file formal extension requests with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The rule applies primarily to two groups: roughly 1.2 million F-1 student visa holders and approximately 300,000 J-1 exchange visitors annually. Together, they account for some of the most productive contributors to the U.S. research enterprise and economy. According to the Brookings Institution, the regulation drew over 20,000 public comments during its comment period — an unusually high number for what DHS framed as a procedural change.

Why Four Years Is Not Enough

The four-year cap creates an immediate problem for graduate students. More than half of first-time bachelor's degree recipients in the U.S. take longer than four years to finish, according to federal data. The median doctoral student spends nearly six years completing a dissertation, with some programs stretching beyond seven. Under the new rule, a Ph.D. student who follows every rule and excels academically will still face the bureaucratic uncertainty of a USCIS extension application before finishing their degree.

"This annual cost is more than 22 times the cumulative total cost DHS identifies as the ten-year cost of the rule. It equates to the loss the U.S. economy would suffer from the disappearance of the entire economy of Delaware or New Hampshire."

— National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine Report

The impact extends to international physicians. The International Medical Graduate Taskforce stated bluntly that "it would be impossible" for physicians to complete critical training programs in general surgery, geriatrics, or cardiology within four years. International physicians account for nearly 25% of the U.S. physician workforce, and many serve in medically underserved areas.

The Economic Cost

A report commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences estimated the regulation could impose annual losses of $72–145 billion over ten years by deterring international students and researchers from choosing the United States. The authors surveyed roughly 1,000 current international Ph.D. students and postdoctoral fellows: approximately half said they either "definitely" or "probably" would not have come to the U.S. if they had known duration of status would be eliminated.

International students contribute $42.9 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support over 355,000 American jobs, according to NAFSA. Education-related travel service exports were valued at $53.58 billion in 2024 by the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

What Indian Students Should Know

India is the second-largest source of international students in the United States, with Indians representing a disproportionate share of STEM graduate programs — exactly the population most affected by this rule. Indian students pursuing Ph.D.s in engineering, computer science, or the biological sciences will now face a four-year clock from the moment they arrive, with no guarantee that USCIS will process extensions in time for them to continue their research.

The rule also creates new friction for the OPT pathway — the post-graduation work authorization that many Indian graduates use as a bridge to H-1B sponsorship. Combined with the recently proposed $100,000 H-1B fee and heightened scrutiny across visa categories, the cumulative effect narrows the pipeline from Indian university to American workplace at nearly every stage.

Students already enrolled in U.S. programs are not grandfathered; the rule applies to all current and future F-1 and J-1 holders. Universities are expected to begin adjusting their international student advisement to reflect the new requirements, though USCIS has not yet clarified processing timelines or adjudication standards for the extension applications.
